Description_Simple.comparison_text:
Title: Balanced Delimiter Checker

Main Goal: Verify whether a given string has properly matched and nested parentheses ‘()’, braces ‘{}’, and brackets ‘[]’.

Description:  
The class ExpressionChecker provides a single static method checkExpression(String) that:
1. Rejects the string immediately if its length is odd (cannot be fully paired).  
2. Iterates over each character, pushing any opening delimiter ‘(’, ‘{’, or ‘[’ onto a stack.  
3. Upon encountering a closing delimiter ‘)’, ‘}’, or ‘]’, it checks if the stack is empty (unmatched closer) and then pops the last opening.  
4. Compares the popped opening to the current closing; any mismatch returns false.  
5. If the loop completes without errors, it returns true only if the stack is empty (all delimiters matched).  
This ensures the expression’s delimiters are balanced and properly nested.

Description_Simple.comparison_text:
Title: K Smallest Sum Pairs Finder
Main goal: Given two sorted integer arrays and an integer k, efficiently compute the k pairs (one element from each array) whose sums are the smallest.

This code defines a method kSmallestPairs(int[] nums1, int[] nums2, int k) that:
1. Returns an empty list if either array is empty or k ≤ 0.
2. Uses a min-heap (PriorityQueue) keyed by the sum of a candidate pair.
3. Initially offers the pair (nums1[0], nums2[0]) with its sum.
4. Repeatedly polls the smallest-sum pair, adds it to the result, and pushes its "right" neighbor (same row, next column) and, for the very first column element, its "down" neighbor (next row, same column), ensuring all potential next-smallest sums are considered.
5. Stops once k pairs are collected or the heap is exhausted.
6. Returns the list of k smallest-sum pairs.

mbpp_0747.reference_description: Write a function to find the longest common subsequence for the given three string sequence.

Description_Simple.reference_text: Write a function to find the longest common subsequence for the given three string sequence.
Description_Simple.comparison_text:
Title: Longest Common Subsequence for Three Strings (LCS3)

Main Goal:
Compute the length of the longest common subsequence shared by three input strings.

Description:
This code defines a method `lcsOfThree(String s1, String s2, String s3)` that uses a three-dimensional dynamic programming table `dp[i][j][k]` to build up, for all prefixes of the three strings, the length of their longest common subsequence. It iterates through every index triplet (i, j, k), setting `dp[i][j][k] = 0` if any index is zero, otherwise:
- If the current characters `s1[i–1]`, `s2[j–1]`, and `s3[k–1]` all match, it takes `dp[i–1][j–1][k–1] + 1`.
- If they do not all match, it takes the maximum of excluding one character from one of the strings: the max of `dp[i-1][j][k]`, `dp[i][j-1][k]`, and `dp[i][j][k-1]`.

Finally, it returns `dp[length1][length2][length3]`, which is the LCS length for the full strings.

Description_Simple.comparison_text:
This class defines a method getTotalNumberOfSequences(n, k) that builds a 2D DP table dp[i][j] for 0≤i≤n and 0≤j≤k satisfying:
- dp[i][j] = 0 if i<j or i==0 or j==0,
- dp[i][1] = i (any single element from 1 to i),
- dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[floor(i/2)][j-1] for j>1.

The recurrence counts all length-j sequences whose last element is ≤i: either the last element is <i (dp[i-1][j]) or exactly i (in which case the prior j−1 elements must lie in [1…⌊i/2⌋], given the “next ≥ 2×prev” rule). The result dp[n][k] is returned as the total number of such “doubling” sequences of length k bounded by n.

- Finally returns `ways[amount][numCoins-1]`, the total number of combinations.

Title: Woodall Number Checker

Main goal: Determine whether a given long integer is a Woodall number (of the form k·2^k − 1).

Summary: The `isWoodall` method first rules out even inputs (only odd numbers can be Woodall) and treats 1 as a special case (1 = 1·2^1−1). For any other odd input N, it increments N by 1 to get N+1, then repeatedly divides by 2 while counting how many times (k). If after k divisions the remaining quotient equals k, then N+1 = k·2^k and N = k·2^k−1, so the method returns true. Otherwise it returns false.

Title: Super Ugly Number Generator

Main Goal: Compute the n-th “super ugly” number—numbers whose only prime factors come from a given list of primes—using a min-heap to efficiently merge the sequences of multiples while skipping duplicates.

Summary:
This code implements the classic “merge k sorted lists” approach to generate super ugly numbers in ascending order. It maintains:
- An array `ugly[]` where `ugly[0] = 1`, building up to `ugly[n–1]`.
- A priority queue of `Node` objects, each tracking a prime, its current multiple value, and an index into `ugly[]`.
In each step, it:
1. Polls the smallest current candidate from the heap.
2. If it’s different from the last accepted ugly number, appends it to `ugly[]`.
3. Advances that node’s index, recomputes its next multiple, and re-inserts it into the heap.
Once `n` ugly numbers are found, it returns the last one.

Title: FactorialLastDigit

Main Goal:
Compute the last decimal digit of the product of all consecutive integers from a given start (l) + 1 up to an end (r), i.e. the last digit of r! / l!.

How it Works:
1. If l equals r, the product is empty so it returns 1.
2. If r – l ≥ 5, the result will include a factor of 10, so it returns 0 immediately.
3. Otherwise, it multiplies each number (mod 10) from l+1 through r, taking the running product mod 10 to keep only the last digit.
4. Finally, it returns that last digit.

This decompiled Java class defines a single static method, oddDays(int years), intended to calculate how many days remain (“odd days”) when the total days over a span of years is divided by 7. It applies the Gregorian rules for leap years:
- Every 4th year is a leap year.
- Every 100th year is not, unless it is also every 400th year.

Steps in oddDays():
1. Count complete centuries (years/100) and complete 400-year cycles (years/400).
2. Count all 4-year cycles (years/4) to estimate leap years.
3. Adjust the leap-year and non-leap-year counts by subtracting centuries and adding back 400-year cycles, since every 100th year is not a leap year except every 400th.
4. Compute total odd days as (nonLeapYears × 1 day + leapYears × 2 days) and return that result modulo 7.

Note: The decompiled code has imprecise variable names and a stray var5_5 reference, but its goal is to implement the standard leap-year odd-day calculation.

- Finally, it returns the computed value for J(n).

Title: RectangleSquares – Counting Squares in a Rectangle

Main Goal:
The code computes the total number of axis-aligned squares that can be formed inside an IlIllllllllllll × lIIllllllllllll rectangle.

How It Works:
1. The method `countSquares(a, b)` takes two side lengths a and b.
2. It ensures `l` = min(a, b) and `l2` = max(a, b).
3. It applies the closed‐form formula:
   • Sum of squares in the smaller dimension: l*(l+1)*(2l+1)/6  
   • Plus additional rectangles when the larger side exceeds the smaller: (l2–l)*l*(l+1)/2  
4. Returns the total count of all possible squares.
